outcomes.absoluteFailure:
In the ancient libraries of Gondor, certain collections devoted to the servants of the Shadow liken Wargs to the Werewolves that appear in the tales of the First Age. These writings describe beasts whose corporeal forms were subjected to the powers of Morgoth, then inhabited by malevolent spirits unable to recover their former shapes. Wargs would be descended from these creatures, perpetuating through the ages an existence foreign to natural laws. Their appearance as great wolves would conceal a supernatural essence that ordinary weapons could not permanently harm. Wounds inflicted upon their bodies might slow their movements or momentarily destroy their outward form, but the spirit animating them would remain capable of taking shape again when its strength had been restored.

The traditions arising from this interpretation attach particular importance to ancient weapons and words handed down by the Elves. Blades forged according to the arts of the Eldar, weapons consecrated during the wars against the Shadow, and certain names used in the ancient tongues would possess the power to sever the bond uniting a Warg's spirit to its body. Scholars defending this doctrine believe that ordinary warriors may scatter a pack, but that only the power contained in such weapons can destroy its members for good. Several military accounts are interpreted in the light of this belief: when a pack returns after defeat, its survivors are said in truth to be the same spirits that have assumed bodily form once more. Wargs would thus belong to a lesser order of Werewolves, subject to the same supernatural laws as their ancestors.
outcomes.failure:
The Dúnedain of Gondor preserve ancient accounts of the great wolves that accompany the servants of the Shadow. Military chronicles describe swift and powerful creatures, capable of following a trail over long distances and fighting beside Orcs. Some Wargs serve as mounts, while others accompany armed bands as scouts and pursuers. Their intelligence surpasses that of natural animals, and testimony attributes to them a remarkable capacity to recognise weaknesses in a defence. Historians also know older traditions associating certain wolf-like creatures with the powers of Morgoth and the wars of the First Age.

You also know an interpretation according to which Wargs are a lesser form of the Werewolves of old, whose powers have diminished through successive generations. Their language would be a remnant of the speech once possessed by evil spirits, while their collective organisation would arise from a will inherited from the powers that created them. Packs would therefore be bound by a deep obedience to the servants of the Shadow, even when they appear to act alone. Accounts of independent gatherings would be explained by the fulfilment of orders received long before, or by the influence exerted from afar by the masters of the Orcs. This interpretation leads certain scholars to believe that Wargs possess genuine intelligence, but that their will remains wholly subordinate to the dark powers from which they draw their origin.
outcomes.partialSuccess:
The traditions of the Dúnedain of Gondor distinguish Wargs from ordinary wolves by their intelligence, language, and ancient association with Orcs. These great canids possess considerable strength, great endurance, and keen senses that enable them to pursue travellers over long distances. Some serve as mounts for Orc warriors, while others accompany their bands as scouts or pursuers. Historical accounts attribute to them a malice exceeding the necessities of hunting, as well as an ability to recognise the movements of their adversaries and organise their attacks.

You also know that Wargs possess their own language, made up of cries and howls whose meanings generally escape Men. They can gather, exchange warnings, and act in concert without constantly receiving a rider's orders. The traditions preserved within the great families of Gondor associate them with the malevolent creatures whose presence accompanies wars against the servants of the Shadow. They nevertheless distinguish Wargs from the Werewolves mentioned in accounts of the Elder Days, even when certain legends ascribe to both groups an origin connected with the corruption of living beings.
outcomes.success:
The Dúnedain of Gondor preserve a developed knowledge of Wargs, passed down through military chronicles, accounts of the ancient kingdoms, and the traditions of families who perpetuate the Númenórean inheritance. These creatures have the appearance of great wolves, yet their intelligence and language enable them to pursue independent designs. Wargs acknowledge their own leaders, gather to deliberate, and can prepare common enterprises before joining their Orcish allies. Their association with the latter rests upon shared interests and hostility towards the Free Peoples. Some serve as mounts, while others fight within packs that retain their own organisation.

The military traditions of the Dúnedain attach particular importance to distinguishing movements commanded by an Orcish force from those organised by a pack itself. Wargs can recognise the disposition of a defence, follow an adversary's movements, and seek the passages offering the best opportunities of approach. Their language facilitates coordination among several individuals, while their senses enable them to keep the trail of enemies attempting to retreat. A pack may break off an attack, disperse its members, then gather them elsewhere. Men-at-arms familiar with these accounts know that the disappearance of Orcish riders leaves foes still capable of changing their plans and pursuing purposes of their own.

Dúnedain scholars also distinguish traditions concerning Wargs from those relating to the Werewolves of the Elder Days. The tales of the First Age speak of beings connected with evil spirits that served Morgoth, whereas Wargs are known through their corporeal presence, their language, and their alliances with Orcs. Certain traditions attribute their origins to an ancient corruption of wolves, without this explanation being sufficient to equate them with Werewolves. The surest knowledge concerns their behaviour, their organisation, and testimony passed down by those who encountered them. Interpretations of their supernatural nature belong to an older body of tales, whose different versions must be kept distinct.
outcomes.absoluteSuccess:
The deepest knowledge of the Dúnedain of Gondor rests upon a tradition joining the study of ancient tales with the memory of wars against the servants of the Shadow. Wargs appear therein as wolf-like creatures possessing an intelligence and a language that enable them to form designs of their own. Their collective organisation includes leaders, gatherings, and common decisions. Their alliance with Orcs is cooperation between beings capable of pursuing convergent aims, rather than a simple relationship between warriors and their mounts. Wargs may take part in raids, reconnoitre routes, and pursue fugitives, yet their packs retain the ability to act independently of their allies. This autonomy appears in tales of gatherings where Wargs deliberate among themselves and choose the enterprises in which they will take part.

Dúnedain schooled in military history recognise the consequences of this intelligence for the conduct of an engagement. A pack may test several parts of a defence, follow the movements of a force, and seek circumstances that allow an adversary to be isolated. Its members communicate with one another and can coordinate their movements even when separated by the relief or vegetation. Their speed favours changes of direction and pursuits, while their endurance enables them to maintain pressure upon travellers or retreating soldiers for a long time. Wargs also recognise obstacles, defensive dispositions, and the reactions of their enemies. Accounts of war that attribute concerted attacks to them thus describe opponents capable of choosing the ground and altering their plans, rather than animals whose movements depend exclusively upon a rider's orders.

The oldest historical traditions finally establish a distinction between the different wolf-like creatures associated with the Shadow. The Werewolves appearing in tales of the First Age belong to a history bound up with Morgoth's powers and evil spirits. Wargs, whose intelligence and alliances are known from testimony more directly accessible, have a different nature in the accounts that concern them. Certain traditions ascribe their origins to an ancient curse that altered a strain of wolves, while others describe a malevolent spiritual presence attached to their corporeal form. Scholars studying these versions distinguish properties actually observed among Wargs from powers attributed to supernatural beings of the Elder Days. Tales of bodies vanishing after their destruction give rise to such questions, but do not, by themselves, establish that Wargs possess all the properties of Werewolves or of undead beings created by sorcery.

This deeper knowledge also enables an understanding of the diversity of testimony preserved by the peoples of Middle-earth. Hunters principally describe the tracks, movements, and behaviour of Wargs; soldiers emphasise their ability to fight beside Orcs; the traditions of the Elves and the ancient kingdoms illuminate accounts of their origins. Dúnedain capable of bringing these different perspectives together gain a fuller understanding of their nature. They recognise in the Warg a corporeal, intelligent, and malevolent being whose observable abilities are already formidable, while traditions concerning its supernatural origins belong to a more ancient history, harder to establish with certainty.

gmNote: GM verification: absolute failure — confusion with Werewolves and supposed immunity to ordinary weapons; failure — Warg autonomy denied in favour of permanent supernatural obedience; successful results — distinction between historical traditions, ability to deliberate, independence, and military knowledge. The spiritual interpretation of Wargs is retained as a MERP/ICE development, distinct from Tolkien's explicit accounts.
